$comment: Phase 14 evaluation labels, written 2026-10-28 together with fixtures/phase14/eval-app, BEFORE any Phase 14 scoring and before any CommitRift command was run on this application. Author: an AI assistant (Claude) working independently of the Phase 14 implementation: it did not read crates/, runtime/ or docs/phase14/; it read only the Phase 2-13 documents, the Phase 12 fixtures, the Phase 13 evaluation set and scorer, and the midday contracts. No independent human review performed. A label says whether the entry, under the stated environment, can violate the stated property according to PostgreSQL semantics (READ COMMITTED unless `isolation` says otherwise) and JavaScript semantics; `class` is the hazard family a correct discovery should report; `family` the source construct the case exercises; `effectful` whether extraction should bind at least one database write on a reachable path; `tables` the tables the entry touches (including parents read by foreign-key checks); `pairedWith` (when present) the entry the labeled one runs concurrently with (otherwise two invocations of the entry itself); `observable` (when present) says the property is about what callers are told (return value / response), not about table contents; `replicas` (when present) the read-replica routing the label depends on; `requiresDeclaration` (when present) says the property cannot be read from the source or schema and must be declared to be checked, and `declaredInContracts` whether eval-app/commitrift-contracts.json declares it; `contractsUsed` the contract items the environment or property relies on. `why` is the reason: for a positive the violating schedule (or crash/retry sequence), for a negative why no schedule violates the property. Labels are frozen (fixtures/phase14/FROZEN.json): do not edit them to improve metrics; corrections go into `corrections` with a reason.

families.arrays: bounded literal arrays guarding or feeding a write: for-of, .map into values([...]), .includes guard, inArray(literal) in an UPDATE's WHERE
families.strings: template literals, concatenation, startsWith/length/trim/toLowerCase, split of a known constant string
families.multi-row-insert: db.insert(t).values([{...}, {...}]) as one statement, resubmitted after a lost response
families.zod: schema.parse / safeParse feeding a check-then-act; the transform (trim, toLowerCase) changes the value written
families.higher-order: the application's withRetry(async () => ...) around a non-idempotent vs an idempotent write; withAuth(async (ctx) => ...) route handlers
families.replica: drizzle withReplicas: a check on the replica then a write on the primary vs the same check via $primary
families.return-value: properties of what callers are told (at most one told success; read-your-writes), declared and undeclared variants
families.fk-parent-child: parent DELETE x child INSERT under a NO ACTION foreign key; soft-deleted parent x child INSERT
families.timestamp: a lease with expiry compared against a fixed `now` argument; defaultNow / $onUpdate columns
families.json: a jsonb settings document: a property of it as a guard; read-merge-write vs jsonb || in SQL
families.atomic-update: read-modify-write vs SET col = col + n; READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ transaction
families.unique: check-then-insert without a unique key, with a unique constraint, with a partial unique index
families.unsupported: raw SQL whose text or identifier is a runtime argument

foreignKeys.$comment: SQL names; every foreign key is ON DELETE NO ACTION, ON UPDATE NO ACTION, NOT DEFERRABLE. slots.reserved_by, shifts.worker_id and jobs.locked_by are plain columns.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one role grant per (account, member email, role)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same account and member email, the member having no grants, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: for-of over the literal array DEFAULT_ROLES (two iterations); each iteration SELECTs the grant and INSERTs it if absent, as separate autocommitted statements, and role_grants has no unique constraint. Schedule: A and B both SELECT 'viewer' (none), A INSERTs 'viewer', B INSERTs 'viewer': two 'viewer' grants (likewise 'commenter'). The INSERTs' foreign-key checks take FOR KEY SHARE on the account row, which do not conflict with each other.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one api_scopes row per (account, scope)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same account, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: DEFAULT_SCOPES.map(...) builds two rows for ONE statement: INSERT ... VALUES (..), (..) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; (account_id, scope) is the primary key. If B's INSERT meets a key A inserted but has not committed, it waits for A, then skips the row (A committed) or inserts it (A rolled back). The primary key alone rules out a duplicate (without ON CONFLICT the loser would fail with 23505); both statements insert the keys in the same order, so they cannot deadlock either.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: the concurrent claims together record at most one 'assigned' event for the ticket (the ticket is given to at most one agent)
cases.environment: two concurrent claims of one 'open' ticket with no events, by different agents, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: CLAIMABLE.includes(ticket.status) tests the value of a plain SELECT. Schedule: A and B both read 'open' and pass the test; A UPDATEs (assignee A) and INSERTs its event; B's UPDATE, which has no condition on status, overwrites the assignee with B and B INSERTs a second 'assigned' event. Both calls return true; the ticket ends assigned to B with two 'assigned' events.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: the concurrent claims together record at most one 'assigned' event for the ticket
cases.environment: two concurrent claims of one 'open' ticket with no events, by different agents, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: UPDATE tickets ... WHERE id = $1 AND status IN ('open', 'reopened') RETURNING id: the literal array becomes the IN list. If A's UPDATE is uncommitted, B's UPDATE waits for the row lock and, under READ COMMITTED, re-evaluates its WHERE on A's committed version (status 'assigned'): no row, so B returns false and inserts no event. If A committed first, B's snapshot already sees 'assigned'. A crash between A's UPDATE and its INSERT leaves zero events, which satisfies the property.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one invoice run per run key (account, period)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same account and a valid period such as '2026-10', READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The startsWith('20') / length 7 guard passes for '2026-10'; the run key is the template literal `invoice:${accountId}:${period}`, equal for both calls. SELECT by run_key, then INSERT, as two autocommitted statements; invoice_runs_run_key is a plain, non-unique index. Both calls see no run and both insert one.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one export job per (account, normalized format)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same account whose formats normalize to the same extension (e.g. 'CSV' and ' csv'), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: trim().toLowerCase() maps both formats to 'csv', so both calls build the same concatenated key 'export:' + accountId + ':csv', which is the primary key of export_jobs. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (job_key) DO NOTHING: the second INSERT waits for the first's uncommitted key, then inserts nothing (queued: false).

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one beta_signups row and at most one waitlist row per account
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same account, the build as written (RELEASE = 'stable/2026.10'), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: RELEASE.split('/')[0] is the known string 'stable', so the enrollment branch is unreachable; it is a check-then-insert into beta_signups (no unique constraint) that WOULD duplicate if it ran. The reachable branch is INSERT INTO waitlist ... ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO NOTHING with account_id as the primary key: at most one row. A discovery that does not evaluate the split of the constant and explores the beta branch reports a false positive.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one stage per (project, name) (declared one-stage-per-name)
cases.environment: the multi-row INSERT commits and the process crashes before the response is sent; the client resubmits the same request (declared retry on-crash)
cases.why: values([...]) is ONE INSERT statement with three rows (atomic: all or none). After it committed, the resubmitted INSERT adds three more rows with new serial ids; stages has no unique constraint, so 'todo', 'doing' and 'done' each appear twice for the project.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one priority per (project, name) (declared one-priority-per-name)
cases.environment: the INSERT commits and the process crashes before the response; the client resubmits (declared retry on-crash); also two overlapping submissions, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: One INSERT of two rows with ON CONFLICT (project_id, name) DO NOTHING against UNIQUE(project_id, name). The resubmission conflicts on both rows and inserts nothing (it then reports priorities: 0, a misleading response that is not the labeled property). An overlapping submission waits for the first's uncommitted keys, then skips them. A crash before the commit rolls back every row.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one tag per (account, normalized name)
cases.environment: two concurrent submissions of the server action for the same account with names that normalize alike (e.g. ' Urgent' and 'urgent'), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: tagInput.parse(input) returns the TRANSFORMED value (trimmed, lowercased): both calls check and insert 'urgent', which differs from the first raw input. SELECT, then INSERT, autocommitted; tags has no unique constraint. Both see no tag and both insert 'urgent'. (Identical raw inputs duplicate the same way.)

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one category per (account, normalized name)
cases.environment: two concurrent submissions of the server action for the same account with names that normalize alike (e.g. ' Work' and 'WORK'), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: safeParse(input).data carries the transformed name, so both calls use 'work'. UNIQUE(account_id, name) with ON CONFLICT (account_id, name) DO NOTHING: when both pass the SELECT, the second INSERT waits for the first's uncommitted row, then inserts nothing, and the call re-reads the committed winner. Without the trim/lowercase transform the raw names would be distinct keys; with it the constraint covers them.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one signup credit per account (declared one-signup-credit)
cases.environment: the first INSERT commits on the server but the connection fails before its result reaches the client (the driver rejects with ECONNRESET or ETIMEDOUT); withRetry runs the callback again
cases.why: withRetry (defined in src/lib/retry.ts) treats ECONNRESET/ETIMEDOUT as retryable (RETRYABLE.includes(code)) and calls the operation again on a pool connection. The retried INSERT has grant_key NULL; the unique constraint on grant_key is NULLS DISTINCT and nothing else constrains (account_id, reason). The account ends with two signup credits.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one signup credit per account (declared one-signup-credit)
cases.environment: as P14-E12, including a retry that overlaps a still-running first attempt (client-side timeout), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: grant_key = `signup:${accountId}` is unique and the INSERT has ON CONFLICT (grant_key) DO NOTHING. A retry after the commit inserts nothing; a retry overlapping an uncommitted first attempt waits for it, then does nothing (or inserts, if the first rolled back). Every row this entry writes carries the account's key, so there is at most one.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one trial per account
cases.environment: two concurrent POST /api/trials requests of the same signed-in account, the account having no trial, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: withAuth awaits the callback once per request with ctx.accountId from the session. The callback SELECTs the account's trial, then INSERTs one, autocommitted; trials.account_id has no unique constraint and the INSERTs' foreign-key checks (FOR KEY SHARE on the account row) do not conflict. Both requests see no trial and both insert.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one trial per account
cases.environment: two concurrent POST /api/v2/trials requests of the same signed-in account, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: Inside one transaction the callback locks the account row FOR UPDATE, then checks and inserts. The second request's FOR UPDATE waits until the first commits; under READ COMMITTED its trial SELECT is a new statement with a new snapshot and sees the first trial, so it returns started: false. The INSERT's foreign-key check needs FOR KEY SHARE on the account row, which its own transaction already holds more strongly. (Not under REPEATABLE READ: the second transaction's snapshot is taken by its blocked FOR UPDATE, before the first commit, and the row was only locked, not updated, so no 40001 is raised and the check misses the first trial; that environment is not the labeled one.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one ledger posting per invoice
cases.environment: two consecutive runs for the same draft invoice (declared: runs never overlap); the second starts after the first returned and before the asynchronous replica replayed the first run's commit
cases.why: The status check reads the replica; the posting INSERT and the status UPDATE run in one transaction on the primary. The second run still reads status 'draft' from the lagging replica and posts the invoice again; postings.invoice_id is not unique. No concurrency is needed.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one ledger posting per invoice
cases.environment: two consecutive runs for the same draft invoice (declared: runs never overlap); the replica lags; a run may crash at any point
cases.why: The check reads replicatedDb.$primary, i.e. the primary. Runs do not overlap (declared), so the second run's SELECT sees the first run's committed status 'final' and returns false. The posting and the status change commit together, so a crash cannot leave a posting next to a 'draft' invoice. (With overlapping runs the check would race; the contract excludes them.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one caller is told it reserved the slot (declared one-caller-told-reserved)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls by different accounts for one free slot, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the concurrent calls returns true

cases.why: Both SELECTs see reserved_by NULL, both run the unconditional UPDATE, both return true. The table ends with one holder (the last writer), so only the return values show the violation.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one caller is told it reserved the slot (declared one-caller-told-reserved-atomic)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls by different accounts for one free slot, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the concurrent calls returns true

cases.why: UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND reserved_by IS NULL RETURNING id. The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock and, under READ COMMITTED, re-evaluates the WHERE on the committed version (reserved_by set): 0 rows, so it returns false; if the first committed earlier, its snapshot already excludes the row.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one caller is told it got the shift (NOT declared)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls by different workers for one unclaimed shift, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the concurrent calls returns true

cases.why: As P14-E18: both SELECTs see worker_id NULL, both UPDATE unconditionally, both return true; the table ends with one worker. Positive by semantics, but the property is about return values and this application does not declare it, so a tool that infers no return-value property cannot check it.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: read-your-writes: the call is never told its display name was not saved (declared display-name-read-your-writes: no call returns false)
cases.environment: a single call for an existing account whose stored display name differs from the argument, no concurrent rename; the asynchronous replica has not yet replayed the UPDATE
cases.why: The UPDATE autocommits on the primary; the SELECT is routed to the replica, which still returns the old name, so the comparison is false and the call returns false although its write committed.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: read-your-writes: the returned timezone is the timezone this call wrote (NOT declared)
cases.environment: a single call for an existing account whose stored timezone differs from the argument, no concurrent change; the asynchronous replica has not yet replayed the UPDATE

observable.description: the returned value equals the timezone argument

cases.why: As P14-E21: the read-back goes to the lagging replica and returns the old timezone. Positive by semantics; the property is not declared by this application.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no task references a project that does not exist (no orphan task)
cases.environment: addTask concurrent with purgeProject of the same project, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: tasks.project_id REFERENCES projects(id) ON DELETE NO ACTION, so the existence check is redundant for this property. If addTask's INSERT holds FOR KEY SHARE on the project row, purgeProject's DELETE of the project waits for it; after addTask commits, the NO ACTION check finds the task and purgeProject fails with 23503 and rolls back. If addTask's INSERT comes after the DELETE (committed or not), its foreign-key check waits for or sees the deletion and fails with 23503, which addTask maps to { ok: false }. If the task committed between purgeProject's task DELETE and its project DELETE, the NO ACTION check (fresh snapshot under READ COMMITTED) sees it: 23503 again. The database rejects one side; this is a constraint error the application handles (addTask) or surfaces (purgeProject), not a violation of the labeled property.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: no open task belongs to an archived (soft-deleted) project
cases.environment: addTaskIfActive concurrent with archiveProject of the same active project, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: Archiving only sets projects.archived_at, so the foreign key never fires. archive's UPDATE of the project takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE (archived_at is in no unique index), which does not conflict with the FOR KEY SHARE of the task INSERT's foreign-key check. Schedule: addTaskIfActive reads archived_at NULL; archiveProject sets archived_at, cancels the open tasks (none) and commits; addTaskIfActive INSERTs a task with status 'open'. The archived project keeps an open task. The same happens when the task INSERT is still uncommitted while archive's task UPDATE runs: that statement's snapshot does not contain the task, and it does not wait for it.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no open task belongs to an archived (soft-deleted) project
cases.environment: addTaskIfActiveLocked concurrent with archiveProject of the same active project, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: FOR SHARE on the project row conflicts with archive's FOR NO KEY UPDATE. If addTaskIfActiveLocked locks first, archive's project UPDATE waits until the task commits; archive's task UPDATE is a later statement whose snapshot sees the committed task and cancels it. If archive updates first, FOR SHARE waits until archive commits, then (READ COMMITTED) returns the new row version with archived_at set and the call throws before inserting. The task INSERT's FOR KEY SHARE is covered by its own FOR SHARE. (Two FOR SHARE readers do not exclude each other, but two addTaskIfActiveLocked calls cannot violate this property.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: the concurrent claims together start at most one run of the job (at most one job_runs row per (job, started_at = now))
cases.environment: two concurrent claims of one job (not done, lease NULL or expired: locked_until <= now) by different workers with the same `now`, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The lease test job.lockedUntil > now compares two Date objects (by time value) read by a plain SELECT. Both claims see a free or expired lease, both run the unconditional UPDATE (the second overwrites locked_by and locked_until, and $onUpdate sets updated_at) and both INSERT a run with started_at = now: two workers run the job inside one lease.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: the concurrent claims together start at most one run of the job (at most one job_runs row per (job, started_at = now))
cases.environment: two concurrent claims of one job (not done, lease NULL or expired) by different workers with the same `now`, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: UPDATE jobs SET locked_by, locked_until = now + 60 s ... WHERE id = $1 AND done_at IS NULL AND (locked_until IS NULL OR locked_until <= now) RETURNING id. The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock and re-evaluates the WHERE on the committed version: locked_until = now + 60 s is neither NULL nor <= now, so 0 rows and no run. A crash between the UPDATE and the INSERT leaves the job leased without a run, which satisfies the property. (A claim with a later `now`, after the lease expired, is legitimate and outside the environment.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one onboarding call per account
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for an account whose settings.plan is 'pro', READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The jsonb document is read and its property plan === 'pro' guards a SELECT-then-INSERT into onboarding_calls, which has no unique constraint. Both calls pass the guard, see no call and insert one each. (For a 'free' account neither call writes.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: no lost update: after the calls complete, the settings document has every patched key's new value
cases.environment: two concurrent calls on the same account with patches on different keys (e.g. { theme: 'dark' } and { locale: 'de' }), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: Each call reads the whole jsonb document, merges in JavaScript ({ ...settings, ...patch }) and writes the whole document back. Schedule: A and B read { plan }; A writes { plan, theme }; B writes { plan, locale }. B's SET value is a parameter computed from its stale read, so waiting for A's row lock and re-evaluating does not help: theme is lost.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no lost update: after the calls complete, the settings document has every patched key's new value
cases.environment: two concurrent calls on the same account with patches on different keys, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: UPDATE accounts SET settings = settings || $1::jsonb: PostgreSQL computes the merge from the row version the UPDATE locks. The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock and, under READ COMMITTED, recomputes the SET from the committed version, so both keys survive (|| is a top-level merge, like the spread).

cases.label: positive
cases.property: no lost increment: used = initial used + the units of every completed call
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same account, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: A READ COMMITTED transaction does not protect a read-modify-write. Schedule: A and B read used = u; A writes u + a and commits; B's UPDATE (waiting for A's row lock if needed) writes u + b, a parameter computed from its stale read. Both complete; a's units are lost.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no lost increment: used = initial used + the units of every completed call
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same account, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: SET used = used + $1 in one UPDATE: the second waits for the first's row lock and re-evaluates the expression on the committed row version, so both increments count.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no lost increment: used = initial used + the units of every completed call
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same account; each transaction runs at REPEATABLE READ (set by the code), no application retry
cases.why: If B's snapshot predates A's commit, B's UPDATE of the row A updated fails with 40001 (could not serialize access due to concurrent update), so B does not complete and its units are correctly not counted; if B's snapshot follows A's commit, B reads u + a. Either way the counter equals the sum over completed calls. (One call fails; that is not the labeled property.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one device per (account, fingerprint)
cases.environment: two concurrent POST /api/devices requests with the same body, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: A route handler: the body is read with req.json(), then SELECT, then INSERT, autocommitted. The (account_id, fingerprint) index is not unique. Both requests see no device and both insert (both answer 201).

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one API client per (account, name)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same account and name, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: UNIQUE(account_id, name): when both pass the SELECT, the second INSERT waits for the first's uncommitted row and fails with 23505 when it commits (or at once if it already committed). The losing call throws; the property holds. (Every call succeeding is not the labeled property.)

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one active subscription per account
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same account with no active subscription, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The partial unique index subscriptions_one_active ON subscriptions (account_id) WHERE status = 'active' covers every row this entry inserts (status 'active'). Both pass the SELECT; the second INSERT waits for the first's uncommitted row and fails with 23505. A partial index is not a global constraint on the table, but it enforces exactly the labeled property.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.why: db.execute(sql.raw(statement)): the SQL text is a runtime argument.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.why: db.execute(sql`update ${sql.identifier(table)} set hits = hits + 1 ...`): the table is a runtime argument, so neither the table nor its columns are known.
